maintopic: CONTINUATION OF SUBVENTION POLICY FOR FIVE YEARS

speechtext:
Hon, W. M. Benidickson (Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys): Mr. Speaker, one of the most urgent matters awaiting attention on my appointment has been the situation of the Canadian coal industry. This problem must and will have the most careful and immediate consideration, but it has appeared necessary that some steps be taken now that will end the uncertainty of the last few years and provide stability for a reasonable time.
It is the intention of the present government to introduce during this session legislation that will provide assurance to the coal industry that the existing subvention policy shall be continued for five years. This does not imply that there will be drastic change at the end of the period. It does mean that during this interval the problems will be studied seriously, including the past history and the future prospects of the industry, and the government will develop and apply such policies as may seem appropriate.
28902-5-101
There have been substantial changes in the market for coal in recent years. Large industrial consumers have replaced the railways and householders as the major outlets. These large consumers demand stability in their fuel supply, and assurance of this stability has been offered by competitive fuels. A very large proportion of the output from western and eastern Canadian mines has required subvention assistance to find markets, and this assistance has in the past been provided only on a year to year basis through an item in the estimates in our department. It is clear that if the mines are to be maintained in operation some assurance must be provided that will put them in a competitive position in this industrial market.
The coal industry is today in a more healthy condition than it has been for some years. While production has not increased, there is full time operation in most of the remaining mines with the accruing benefits of full employment and stable wage agreements that are necessary. This provision of continued support is assurance to the miners, their families, the dependant service industries and to the mine owners that they can look forward with confidence to a continuation for some years of these present conditions.
Representations urging a decision of this kind have come to me since my appointment from coal producing companies and the employees' unions in both eastern and western Canada.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF SUBVENTION POLICY FOR FIVE YEARS
speechtext:
I am sure, Mr. Speaker, that we on this side welcome the announcement the minister has just made. We also take note of the fact that he declared that the situation of the coal industry was rather healthy. If that is so, I believe it is due to a large extent to the far sighted policies that were instituted by the former administration. I am sure the minister will be the first to acknowledge that.
During my rather brief tenure of office as minister of mines and technical surveys I had occasion to make a few statements in the house concerning coal subsidies, and particularly in respect of subsidies on coal exported to Japan. As a result of that policy instituted in 1958 our coal exports to Japan, which were practically nil in 1957, reached three quarters of a million tons during the last fiscal year. The industry has acknowledged that this was made possible because of the subsidies paid.

Continuation of Coal Subvention
We welcome the statement that the subsidies will be paid for five years. This provision is in line with the thinking of the former administration, and I believe it will be of great benefit to the coal industry. We will look forward with interest to the legislation the minister has announced. I believe it will prove to be a continuation of that policy of assistance which was one of the features of our administration.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF SUBVENTION POLICY FOR FIVE YEARS
speechtext: All I wish to say in respect of this announcement is that we in this group welcome the statement that legislation will be introduced to continue the subvention policy for five years. We believe that this will, at least in some degree, remove the uncertainties that exist in the coal mining industry as to markets. We welcome the legislation and hope it will have a beneficial effect on this industry.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF SUBVENTION POLICY FOR FIVE YEARS
speechtext: I should like also, Mr. Speaker, to express the appreciation of this party on the fact that this government is apparently going to continue this subsidy for five years instead of having it on a yearly basis as it was in the past. I feel that this is an excellent direction for this government to take. It is going to give a great deal more stability in the areas depending on coal mines than they have had in the past. I hope, too, this is an indication that the government is going to adopt this policy not only for the coal industry but also for various other industries which in the past have suffered from this same sense of instability.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: CONTAINERS
speechtext:
1. Yes, on August 2, 1962, the commission on restrictive trade practices submitted the following reports to the Minister of Justice:
A report on the manufacturing, distribution and sales of paper shipping containers and allied products.
A report concerning the purchase, by Bathurst Power and Paper Company Limited, of Wilson Boxes Limited.
A report concerning the purchase of the common shares of Hendershot Paper Products Limited, by the Canadian International Paper Company.
2.	Each of the preceding reports, copies of which are sent herewith (in the English version, as the printed French version is not yet available), reveals the names of the persons and companies against whom allegations were made in the evidence. The names of all the managers and directors of each firm are not revealed in the reports; but those of some persons, and the positions occupied at certain times are mentioned in the reports and can be found in the appropriate context.
3.	A report concerning the manufacture, distribution, and sales of paper shipping containers and allied products:
(1) "Concerning the agreements that resulted in the fixing of common prices on paper for packing cases and shipping containers, we believe that, under the Combines Investigation Act, it will be possible to ask for a court order preventing those who are taking part in such agreements from keeping them or restoring them later under the same or a modified form. Because of persisting efforts in view of agreements on maintaining a common price for longer periods of time, under

whatever form, the commission thinks that a request should be made, under the Combines Investigation Act, for a sufficiently restrictive order prohibiting the joint employment by the parties to the agreement of any person or any private organization concerned with matters connected with sales prices, cost prices or statistics."
(2) That the most efficient way to restore competition to that industry, as far as production of paper board and containers is concerned, which would be advantageous to the public as it would reduce prices, would be to suppress customs duty both on the paper board and the containers, in the light of the financial situation which existed at the time this report was prepared.
The commission thought that, on the basis of jurisprudence, none of the mergers involved a violation of the Combines Investigation Act. However, it expressed the hope that "in the near future a review will be made of the matters raised by those rulings of the appeal courts, more particularly the Supreme Court of Canada, in order that they may be finalized."
Report on the purchase of Wilson Boxes Limited by Bathurst Power and Paper Company Limited:
The commission felt that on the basis of jurisprudence, this merger was not in violation of the Combines Investigation Act.
In the report concerning shipping containers, the commission recommended that appropriate changes be made in the Customs Tariff to restore competition in the supply of paper board and shipping containers. Such recommendations would also be relevant to this investigation.
Report on the purchase of the common shares of Hendershot Paper Products Limited by the Canadian International Paper Company:
The commission was of the opinion that on the basis of jurisprudence, this merger was not in violation of the Combines Investigation Act.
In the report on shipping containers, the commission recommended that certain amendments be made to the Customs Tariff which in its opinion would protect the public against needlessly high prices both on paper board and shipping containers, which would contribute to eliminate restrictions which inevitably apply to the supply of packing board when a predominant part of the packing board production in Canada is carried out by integrated companies and is used in their own converting operations. The commission feels that the recommendations made in connection with the investigation on shipping containers are relevant to this investigation.

maintopic: C.N.R. WATERFRONT CONSTRUCTION, FORT WILLIAM, ONT.
speechtext:

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
maintopic: POWER SUPPLY, INDIAN AGENCY BUILDINGS, NORWAY HOUSE, MAN.
speechtext:
1. The government's policy to date has been to acquaint Canadians with the facts regarding the nuclear threat and the importance of shelter as a protection against fall-out. A comprehensive program of public information has been used, including the provision of shelter plans of many types, among which there are a number of inexpensive but effective ones. This has been coupled with financial assistance by way of loans under the National Housing Act. This has all been directed to the objective of individual and family effort to provide added protection at home. Any Canadian, on request, can get promptly information set out in readily understandable terms, covering shelters suitable to a great variety of needs and including readily improvised shelter as well. Even the simplest of these arrangements can reduce the fall-out danger markedly.
No government program to build shelters for families, groups or communities has been undertaken.
2. The present government is studying the various possible policies in regard to shelters.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister

speechtext:
1.	Has the government arrived at a decision on (a) what is the best type of individual survival shelter in the event of a nuclear attack (b) what is the best type of community shelter?
2.	If so, what steps, educational and financial, has it taken to ensure the proliferation of such protection?
3.	What success or response has come to these efforts?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
speechtext:
1. (a) and (b) The government has provided, over several years, thorough research into the matter of the best types of shelter for Canadians having in mind the conditions likely to affect this country in nuclear war. From this, designs and structures have been developed, both with respect to home shelters and to the congregate or community type. The designs for such shelters have been published in convenient pamphlets which cover a wide range of fall-out and anti-blast shelters.
The government, further, has had wide surveys made of larger buildings in Canada to determine their potential protection against radioactive fall-out. The emergency measures organization provides information to all who ask for it on measures that can be taken to improve fall-out protection in larger buildings.
2. Through broadcasts, displays, pamphlets and manuals, information on fall-out has been provided for public use. This has cost the federal government more than $630,000 over the last two fiscal years. Provincial and municipal governments further this program of public information by ensuring ready distribution of the material provided by the federal government.
Under the National Housing Act, loans or increases on present mortgages can be provided for home owners in order to build shelters.

1.	Does the Canadian military carry out studies in probability using the theory of games and, if so, has it applied this theory to the probabilities of civilian survival in Canada in the event of a nuclear attack on (a) Canada (b) the U.S.A.?
2.	What are the estimates of civilian population survival resulting from these studies, giving the various modes of attack?

1. Studies have been made but not using the theory of games.
2. These analytical studies involve the use of a great many theoretical variables, including a number of imponderables associated with Canada's position to the main target of attack. These considerations do not lend themselves to an accurate estimate of population survival.

3. (a) Silviculture: The Department of Forestry conducts a comprehensive program of forestry activities on a national scale. This over-all program is aimed at maximizing returns from all resources available. They include:
(i)	Forestry research relating to soils, silviculture, tree improvement and stand management, forest mensuration, and fire protection. Though there is no strictly official common policy adhered to by the federal and provincial governments, activities in the silviculture field are conducted by this department in accordance with programs established through committees which are made up of federal, provincial and industrial representatives. Information from these sources is studied by the department and is available to all persons interested.
A number of provinces depend almost entirely upon the federal research services; other provinces conduct provincial programs in close co-operation with the federal department. One outstanding illustration of this cooperation is the joint research agreement between Ontario and the federal government whereby research resources are pooled in an attack upon problems of mutual interest.
(ii)	Federal-provincial agreements. The federal-provincial forestry agreements provide federal financial assistance to the provinces in the fields of forest inventory, reforestation, stand improvement, forest access, and forest fire protection. All ten provinces are participating in this program. The agreements represent a nation wide recognition by the federal and provincial governments of the need to place special emphasis on these fields.
(iii)	Forest fire protection. That portion of the federal-provincial agreements respecting fire protection, together with the policy whereby provinces may call upon the federal government for armed services' assistance, combine in a policy operative at the national level. This policy is of course concurrent with research pursued at the regional level, and is aimed at establishing local fire danger tables related with type of forest stand, type of fuel, topography and weather factors.
(iv)	Dissemination of information. The department considers it has a function in disseminating scientific, technical and educational information and making it available to forest owners, industry and the general public. In certain areas, such as educational films, it works in close co-operation with provincial authorities, and prints are available to all levels of government. In another area, popular education, a major effort is made by the Canadian Forestry Association, with financial assistance from the federal government.

3. (b) Resource use. In relation to resource use, the Department of Forestry's policy is in the formative stage. The department participates in the resource use program being explored by ARDA.
Another promising area, in which the department has the function of co-ordinating research, is the watershed research program in the Saskatchewan river basin. This project has the support of four federal departments (agriculture, forestry, northern affairs and national resources, transport), two joint agencies (eastern Rockies forest conservation board and the prairie provinces water board), and three Alberta provincial departments (lands and forests, agriculture, research council). The aim of the program is control of water flow based on a multiple use involving forestry, agriculture, mining, recreation, and wildlife; in a more specific sense its goal is watershed protection and maintenance in conjunction with the utilization of forest and other resources.
The Department of Forestry also acts in cooperation with the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources in providing forest surveys and advising on management of the Yukon and Northwest Territories forests, and of the forests of the national parks. Similar service and advice are provided for the Indian reserves which come under the jurisdiction of the Department of Citizenship and Immigration. Management of forested areas in military camps (Gagetown, Valcar-tier, Petawawa, Borden) is directly under this department's authority, as well as management of our own forest experiment stations.

DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS MUNICIPAL LOAN LEGISLATION    MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I desire to ask leave to move the adjournment of the house under standing order 26 for the purpose of discussing a definite matter of urgent public importance.
This question stems from the statement made yesterday in the Quebec legislature by the premier of the province of Quebec, Hon. Jean Lesage, in which he vehemently denounced as a very serious infringement upon provincial autonomy, the proposed federal assistance to municipalities, and various other bills or resolutions submitted to the house by the government.
That statement, following what has been called his fiscal ultimatum, accentuates considerably the general uneasiness within confederation, of which Mr. Lesage said recently that it was being given its last chance.
Mr. Speaker, it is most urgent to discuss this matter immediately.
(Text):

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS MUNICIPAL LOAN LEGISLATION    MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS MUNICIPAL LOAN LEGISLATION    MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the motion introduced by the hon. member for Three Rivers is based on standing order 26. An examination of that section reveals that the adjournment of the house can be moved for the purpose of discussing a definite matter. In my opinion, that is the first point we must consider concerning the advisability of granting or refusing the adjournment of the house.
If we take a close look at the proposal made by the hon. member for Three Rivers, we notice that it concerns in particular the examination of government order No. 5 on
[Mr. Martineau.l

today's order paper, that is Bill C-76 to provide assistance for municipalities. Consequently, the motion for adjournment has a very definite objective.
On the other hand, standing order 26 states further on that the matter must be of public importance.
Now, in this case, we have certainly a matter of public importance, and it is under the jurisdiction of the house, as it is a bill following a resolution which had been submitted to the house, and as it had been completely impossible, while discussing that resolution, to obtain, either from the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) or from the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) any detailed information with regard to the jurisdiction of the federal government on the matter.
The Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefen-baker), the hon. member for Pontiac-Temis-camingue (Mr. Martineau) and others raised the point of the constitutional nature of the bill. Therefore if we refer to Beauchesne's citation No. 100 we find that the conditions for the adjournment of the house are met in the motion of the hon. member for Three Rivers, and the matter of urgency is to be considered, because the discussion of the resolution is not so much a question of dealing with the request of the prime minister of the province of Quebec, as of analysing a bill, a situation which affects the very basis of Canadian confederation, where the future of all provinces is at stake.
Those are the reasons why this question is a definite matter of urgent public importance.
As to the urgency of this debate, I am afraid that Mr. Speaker will declare that we still have a day of budget discussion before us and that this would be the time to deal with the problem; but considering that Wednesday afternoon does not give hon. members much time to study this matter, and that the question period is not yet closed, I feel that such a reason would not be sufficient to justify the rejection of the motion. That is why I respectfully submit that you should grant the request of the hon. member for Three Rivers.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS MUNICIPAL LOAN LEGISLATION    MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
After reading carefully standing order 26, it becomes evident that the motion of the hon. member for Three Rivers is in order but at this stage I fail to see the reason for the intervention of the hon. member for Berthier-Maskinonge-Delanaudiere, because there has not been any indication that the motion was opposed. The motion has not yet been discussed and it has not been opposed by

the government members. I believe, therefore, that his intervention at this stage is untimely and inappropriate.

The second is the administrative responsibility of the government. I would respectfully suggest that a statement made by the premier of another province does not involve the administrative responsibility of the government.
Furthermore, Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Berthier-Maskinonge-Delanaudiere answered his own argument when he said that the house has the right to discuss this matter in the present budget debate; thus, there is no urgency in the proposal of the hon. member for Three Rivers.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in the very few minutes of this debate that are left it is hardly possible to give very much of the material I had intended to bring to the attention of the house. Suffice it to say, however, in view of the shortness of time, that this budget has been the biggest disappointment of any budget introduced in recent years-

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Why did you not vote for the amendment?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
-in that it was no better than any the former government brought in, but that the people of Canada had expected something better. I am convinced that neither of the old parties, with the approach they take to solve Canada's economic problems, has the answers to Canada's economic needs. Otherwise we would not be continually moving in the realm of deficit financing, with higher and higher tax loads.
My attention was drawn the other day to an editorial in the Penticton Herald of June 11 which says:
Our frequent reference to the dangers of long continued federal deficit financing is this one fact-every deficit position makes it cumulatively more difficult to get a balance the next time.
The servicing of the debt, in itself, is an ever tightening strangulation-
Canadians, let's face it, are not willing to make the sacrifices necessary, nor do most legislators know what's happening. Either they don't care, or they're too politically timid to risk their election necks.
Something should be done, Mr. Speaker, if we are to have any hope at all of continuing in the way that a nation such as Canada should. This year the cost of servicing our debt is $93 million more than it was last year, and it will be more next year because inevitably the national debt goes higher and higher.

The Budget-Mr. Thompson
I realize the Minister of Finance has endeavoured to bring the deficit down for the coming year, but the sad part of it is that the policies which he followed and the steps which he took have brought about the very reverse of the condition he intended to bring about, and which should be brought about.
The 11 per cent tax on building materials is a very unfortunate tax addition. I would appeal to the minister, in view of the tremendous objection from right across Canada, to remove this tax from building materials, and do it as soon as possible. Otherwise we will find that not only will unemployment increase but the whole expansion of our economy will grind to a halt, and bring about a situation which certainly will not be in the best interests of the country.

This tax will not only work hardship on home construction but also on many other aspects of the industry. In fact no event in parliament has ever brought so much correspondence across my desk, and I am sure this is true of the Minister of Finance and other hon. members as well. Therefore I appeal to the minister to take some action to correct the situation. Either withdraw the tax completely or else postpone its effective date.
A second matter which I believe to be urgently essential is that new steps must be taken to reach the basic needs of the country so far as its economy is concerned. We are no longer living in an era when there is a problem of production. To all intents and purposes that problem has been solved. Our problem now is one of distribution, and it is a question of how we can increase more effective demand in order to increase our consumption both at home and with respect to our export markets. What Canada needs is a different approach to its economic policies based on the premise that our basic problem is one of distribution and consumption rather than of production. The tax load must be eased, particularly for those in the lower

income brackets; the 11 per cent tax on building materials is going to strike hardest at this level. Furthermore there must be an increase in the effective demand of our people. This can only be accomplished by more purchasing dollars being in their hands in order to consume the production of which we are capable. The tax base must be broadened by the expansion of the economy in such a way that greater taxes are not imposed upon any particular group, but that there is a greater increase in earnings and in the value of our over-all economy so that the load will be lighter for all concerned.
One of the greatest problems that faces our economy today is in the realm of social capital. It has been estimated by economists and by those who are very close to the overall needs of our nation that we require at least $1 billion a year for the next ten years in the realm of social capital. One of the most effective ways of speeding up the expansion of our economy and placing more purchasing power in the hands of wage earners and consumers at large would be to put vast amounts of social capital into the economy to take care of our public needs in the realm of schools, roads, hospitals, bridges, public buildings and this type of project. However, this need not be done through deficit financing if we face the fact that we ought to be using the Bank of Canada to supply this social capital. If this were done the very crux of the problem would be dealt with, and I am convinced we would see the economy moving forward on the basis upon which it should and must move forward if we are going to solve this problem of meeting the financial needs of our governments and at the same time give the incentives for our industry and commerce to move forward.

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR PROGRAM TO ESTABLISH RECREATIONAL FACILITIES
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government, in consultation with the recently formed federal-provincial parks conference, should give immediate consideration to establishing a recreational parks program to:
1.	extend the picnic sites and camp ground program;
2.	complement the national parks system;
3.	meet the growing recreational needs of a changing society;
4.	provide adequate services and facilities for Canada's booming tourist industry.
He said: Mr. Speaker, it is unfortunate that the time to discuss this important motion is going to be limited by circumstances. However, I have been assured already by many members on both sides of the house that there is considerable support for this motion and in view of that fact I shall keep

my remarks as brief as I can in order to allow as many members as possible to take part in the debate during the period of time available.
There has been growing concern in recent years arising from the failure to establish policies that provide for the wise management and the multiple use of our renewable resources. It was because of this growing concern that the former prime minister, now Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker), in the year 1958 in an important policy speech called for the setting up of a national committee or conference on conservation that would deal with the urgent and critical problem of the wise management of our great resource heritage. As a result we had in the city of Montreal in the fall of 1961 that historic conference which became known as the resources for tomorrow conference. Out of that conference came recommendations that will have a significant impact on the utilization and development of our resources for many years to come.
One of the recommendations that came from that conference had to do with the urgent necessity of providing the park facilities required to meet the growing recreational needs of an affluent society. This resolution is merely underlining a policy that has been endorsed by a broad cross-section of Canadians, some 700 in number, who met in that conference; a policy that has been also endorsed by the first federal-provincial conference on park development that took place in Ottawa last October; and a policy that has been widely supported by such voluntary groups as the Audubon society and others interested in the preservation of our renewable resources.
As the resolution indicates, we have a parks program in operation at the moment. We have the national parks program which has operated in Canada since the year 1885. I think the fact that we go back to the year 1885 to mark the establishment of the program is eloquent testimony to the vision and the wisdom of the members of the government of that day who, of course, happened to be members of a Conservative administration. I say this, not with any partisan emphasis at all but only to underline that down through the years since confederation the Conservative party has always emphasized the need for wise management and development of our renewable resources.
The national parks system is still the backbone of our present parks program. It is dedicated in principle, according to the National Parks Act, to the preservation and conservation of our wildlife and our scenic beauty. There has been a slow development of the system over the years. At the present
26, 1963	1615
Request for Parks Recreational Program time there are only 18 such parks and they constitute less than 1 per cent of our total land area. So I think it will be readily seen by all members that we have not been overabundantly supplied in the area of national park development with park facilities of this kind.
I should also like to refer to the excellent programs that have been developed by various provincial governments which are supplementing the functions of the national parks system. However, we have reached a critical stage in our development where urgent action is required to supplement and to complement the national parks program. This is why I have used the words in the resolution that immediate consideration should be given to establishing a recreational parks program because, as I hope to demonstrate in my remarks, the time is long past due when action is required in this area.
I do not have to go into details because I am sure all hon. members have become aware of this difficulty as a result of the informational and educational impact of the resources for tomorrow conference and other recent statements that have been made in this field of activity. We have passed through a social revolution in which mobility has been intensified largely by the construction of modern paved highways and the ubiquitous presence of the automobile which has put everybody on wheels in our affluent society. There are some 66 million vehicles registered in the United States, I understand, and a proportionate number registered in Canada, which has meant that the population has become mobile in a way never before seen in history.
Combined with the factor of mobility is the availability of leisure time. With improved working conditions leisure time, which was once a rare commodity restricted to the well to do in the upper levels of society, has now become available to all. These are the two basic ingredients of the social revolution that have created an almost insatiable demand for expanded recreational facilities; and this is combined with an increase in the tourist population in recent years which can only be described as a population explosion in tourism.
The former administration moved quickly, as I have already indicated, to deal with this problem that had been long neglected.
In the national parks branch, for example, a planning section was established in 1958. There was a recommendation by the planning section that each of the national parks should be carefully surveyed and a master plan developed for each of the parks. The first such plan was announced to the members of the House of Commons last fall when the
1616	HOUSE OF
Request for Parks Recreational Program Overlander report, which dealt with growth problems in our most populous national park, Banff national park, was tabled.
Then, too, last January in the city of Calgary, it was my privilege to announce a new zoning policy for our national parks system which would preserve the fundamental principle of national parks, namely, the conservation of wild life and areas of natural beauty, at the same time providing maximum recreational facilities. In our national park there is to be one third of the park area dedicated to the preservation of wilderness. Other portions of the park will be developed into what might best be called visitors' service centres. These would be carefully planned on the basis of the community plan to which I have already referred, so as to provide minimum impairment of wilderness areas. Then, there would be the general' usage areas. Those are the three major steps that have been taken in the national parks program that I think will have an important influence on the future development of these parks.
Outside the parks branch itself, the voluntary organizations have become increasingly interested in this problem. The nucleus of a national parks association is one of the developments that came out of the resources for tomorrow conference. This was established in Toronto last April, and I heartily congratulate those citizens who have come together in order to deal with the problem of meeting the need for recreational services, resulting in increasing demand for recreational park programs.
Another major development was the federal-provincial' parks conference held last October. At that conference a proposal was made to the provincial representatives that the federal government of that day would be willing to participate in such a program as is outlined in this resolution. The impression I gained from participating in the conference was that all representatives were positively oriented towards the idea.
We have been endeavouring also, of course, to create new national parks. There is a fundamental problem in this regard in that the resources belong to the provinces. Before the federal authority can establish a national park it must have land owned by the provinces made available free of encumbrances. We had made good progress towards getting agreement with the province of Nova Scotia for the establishment of an additional national park there. We were negotiating with the northern territories with a view to establishing suitable park areas there. Of course, many hon. members will be aware that there has


been some consideration of an additional park in the province of British Columbia in the Garibaldi mountain area.
In addition to this, however, and I think this is fundamental to the resolution we have before us, the former government in its planning for the future of resource areas deliberately set out a program for expanding the establishment of historic sites and monuments. Here is an area in Canadian development that has been sadly neglected. I must confess one of the reasons such a program was enunciated and launched was the great interest exhibited by members from all sides of the house as well as from the public in general. There is now well under way in Canada a major program of historic site and park development. This whole program was geared to fit into our centennial celebration. By that year major historic and park restoration will be completed in every part of Canada.
One of the most important of these, is Louisburg, a multi-million dollar restoration program and which is going to have a multiple use in that it will be a major attraction for a growing tourist industry. It will provide recreational activities as well. The Plains of Abraham and the Citadel in Quebec comprise one of our oldest historic sites and is well developed. In Ontario, we have several areas that are under development. The province of Manitoba is co-operating in the restoration of the Fort Garry site. In Saskatchewan, it is Batoche. In Alberta, there are several areas and in B.C. likewise. The former administration, aware of the historic significance of activities in the north, moved to preserve historic Dawson City as a historic site. This is a matter that has come under criticism from hon. members opposite.
There is no reason why any part of Canada should be discriminated against in a program of this kind. There has been a good deal of bias against the development of northern Canada, I know, on the part of the Liberal party ever since the Conservative government announced a program for the vigorous development of this area. I think it must be recognized that Canadian development has always been outward and upward into the great Canadian northwest. One of the greatest epochs in Canadian development was the gold rush into the Yukon, the trail of '98 as it became popularly known and recognized around the world, largely through the writings of Robert Service. This is one aspect of Canadian history that is known in every part of the world, even in the more remote parts. In the days to come, it is going to be one of the major attractions of our booming tourist industry which will bring millions of dollars to the Canadian economy, as an indirect result.

However, the major purpose is to preserve our historic sites and monuments for posterity and at the same time take into consideration the multiple use concept, because these sites have recreational value as well. I can also mention the winter works program which has been used by municipalities to provide for growing recreational needs, particularly in the urban centres. There have been hundreds of recreational park areas established because of the excellent winter works program of the former administration.
ARDA needs no emphasis or interpretation on my part. ARDA, which is now getting underway in every province of Canada, provides as one of its major measures alternative land use. I know in my own province- the province with which I am most familiar -the provincial government is moving forward in several areas to use the provisions of the Agricultural Rehabilitation and Development Act in order to meet the growing demands for recreational parks. This is all fine, but on top of it the demand is so urgent and such a rapidly growing one that I am convinced we, as the parliament of Canada, must move immediately to launch, in cooperation with the provinces-and as I have indicated the matter has already been presented to the first meeting of the federal-provincial conference-to establish a program specifically designed to create recreational park areas in order to deal with some of the problems I have outlined.
Briefly this is the parks and recreational aspects of the matter, and perhaps I should add a word about the economic benefits that would derive from such a program. I know this is always a matter in consideration when governments are moving towards expenditure in some particular area of Canadian life. I believe that if we were to move enthusiastically and expeditiously into this program, any expenditure would be more than paid for by the booming tourist industry that has been talked about so much in recent months. Tourism used to be regarded as of little economic significance-

Mr. Speaker, I am sure it has always been a pleasure for those who followed him previously, as it is for me this evening, to follow the hon. member for Brandon-Souris (Mr. Dinsdale) who was the former minister of the department which I represent as parliamentary secretary. I may say I am very grateful to him for having
Request for Parks Recreational Program introduced the topic of the large outdoors, especially after the last six days, and I am sure each member of the house is grateful to him for bringing a little fresh air into the chamber. It is a refreshing change. But, in any event I was somewhat surprised to find him taking a partisan approach to the problem of recreation, which I think we would all endorse. With respect I would like to remind him that the Conservative party has no monopoly on the north, nor has it a monopoly on the park lands of Canada, except perhaps a blurred vision here and there.
Since this is the first time I have had an opportunity to speak this session may I, sir, through you transfer to His Honour the Speaker my loyalty and congratulations. He is a man of many talents and, as you know, a man with countless friends. He has all the requisite qualities for the office he now holds. He has a sense of fairness, a judicial and even temperament, and a gift of humour. I consider myself fortunate to have had the benefit of his friendship ever since I entered politics.
I had the good fortune to speak at the nomination convention of Mr. Deputy Speaker, the hon. member for Stormont, a year or so ago, and I believe I have the agreement of all hon. members present when I say his position too is a just reward for his capacities. He has already established a good reputation in the chair, even showing courage enough to stand up to the ministry on occasion. To you, sir, as the deputy chairman of committees I also extend my heartiest congratulations.
The motive behind this motion today is the result of a growing urbanized society, a society that will be choked if it cannot break out into the outdoors. That is what I understand the mover to mean when he says in his motion that we must establish a parks program to "meet the growing recreational needs of a changing society". In Canada we have 15 metropolitan centres which contain nearly 40 per cent of our population. It is because of that concentration of population that our people are in need of outdoor recreation We have had an outstanding population growth accompanied by the phenomenon of increased leisure time. We have the increased mobility given to us by the automobile, and although my hon. friend calls it the affluent society, I can say we do have a certain increase in our standard of living. What has been the result of this, and why do I suggest this motion meets with the general endorsement of the house? It is because there has occurred a crisis in recreation, and it is composed largely of urban pressures. This has made our national parks system inadequate.
1618	HOUSE OF
Request jor Parks Recreational Program
If I might cite to the house the figures of the numbers of people who have visited our national parks over the years, I think it will illustrate just what I mean. In 1911 there were 100,000 annual visitors to our national parks; in 1920, 150,000; in 1930, 500,000, and in 1939, a million. Bringing the figures up to date, last year there were 7J million visitors to our national scenic parks.
I have had a projection made for me by the officials of the national parks branch wherein they estimate that this year we will see over 8 million people visit those parks, and in 1970 it is estimated that 10.5 million people will visit our park lands. By 1975 this will increase to 15.5 million people. This, you will appreciate, has put an undue strain on the whole national parks system, and if the house were to allow me the necessary consent to table two charts, I would like to do so. One chart indicates the increase in visitor attendance to our national parks over the past 32 years, and the other chart indicates the increase in the use of national park camp grounds over the past 12 years. I think the house would get a very graphic view from these charts of just how impressive the growth in the use of our parks has been.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR PROGRAM TO ESTABLISH RECREATIONAL FACILITIES
speechtext:
As I have said, this phenomenal' increase has placed undue demands on the facilities of our national parks, because they were not originally established to supply mass recreation. They were established to preserve the wilderness of the country, to preserve sections of this land in its natural state, so that those who came after, and future generations to come, could travel unmolested in virgin timberland and near silent streams in order to re-create themselves, which after all is perhaps the compound from which the word recreation is properly derived. But despite the efforts of the national parks branch-and I would like to take the opportunity to congratulate the men and women who staff this branch, a branch that is understaffed today-the national parks system has become inadequate. Consequently we have in Canada a need to supplement and complement the national parks system. That is, I presume, what the motion refers to. We must extend the national, provincial and other parks systems in this country. We must preserve the areas of Canada that are best suited for recreation while there is still time, while there is still land available and while they still can be preserved without a massive expenditure.


I would suggest then, sir, that we must have a formal recognition by this house of recreation as a vital use of land, of recreation as a renewable land resource. The problem, as the hon. member has quite rightly pointed out, is that the jurisdiction over most of the available land is provincial. We must therefore look toward a co-operative federalism, if you will, to combining and co-ordinating the federal and provincial jurisdictions. It was to that end that the first federal-provincial park conference was held last year which established for the first time a contact between the two levels of government on park matters. Because there is a common problem my suggestion to the house would be that a conference or a series of conferences from year to year or every second year is no longer enough; that we should set up a permanent federal-provincial secretariat in charge of co-ordinating the planning, development and use of parkland, which would also be in charge of developing new lands. This secretariat would be a clearing house as well, so that some of the less favoured provinces could benefit from the experience of those which have been more blessed by nature and wealth. I said that time is of the essence because unless these lands are set aside for recreation now, mineral, forest and hydroelectric development will assume an early control over these lands and deprive them forever from the use of the citizenry of this country as a means of enjoying leisure time.
What is a national park? I have already said that it is a wilderness area where nature is preserved in its natural state. It can only be preserved if alternate and intermediate areas of recreation are immediately developed so that the boating, hiking and other more mechanized forms of recreation can be put into this type of land so that the national parks can be preserved in their sanctity. There are dangers to our parklands today. Commercialism is one. The pressures of profit must not be allowed to scar the beauties of this country. I would urge the house in its consideration of this problem to recommend, in conjunction with the provinces, at some future date, that the countryside be zoned so that private enterprise untramelled and unrestrained will not, helter-skelter, scar the countryside to the detriment of the general common weal. The parks have another enemy, the machine age. The very automobile that allows people to get there also tends to encroach on the sanctity of the parkland. There are dangers of too easy an access, because we do not have respect for what we do not have to work for. I can remember the chagrin I had in northern Ontario in the Temagami area at one time when with two friends of mine we spent over a week and a half to

canoe into lake Florence right in the Gow-ganda area. After we had been fishing there for two days an airplane landed with three or four fishermen who had taken about an hour and a half from Toronto to get to the same source of nature's bounty that had taken us a week and a half to reach. The private occupation of the key areas of some public lands of our national parks is also a hazard. I would think that the house would want to endorse a policy to the effect that public land in the national parks must remain open to the ordinary citizen and must not be blocked by those who have been allowed over past years to build cottages and shacks and put up tents on a yearly leasehold basis until they consider the land almost their own and impede its access to the ordinary man, woman and child. I say this because the national parks are surely dedicated to all the people of Canada and are maintained by the general taxpayer for public use. It is not the purpose of the national parks to provide summer residential subdivisions, cottage lots or shack-tent areas for the exclusive use and possession of private individuals.
The people who will benefit from future recreation are the generations to come. Sometimes, Mr. Speaker, out of the mouths of babes wisdom is ordained and strengthened. I have here a colour book with certain little essays prepared by the children of the Banff composite high school at Banff national park, which was the first of our national parks. I would like to commend the teacher of this seventh grade social studies class, Mrs. Kathleen McAuley who had, if I might say so, the good sense to ask her pupils to tell her, the country and themselves what they thought the purpose of a national park should be. One little boy, Phillip Elliott, wrote this
Request for Parks Recreational Program and I think it is perhaps as good a definition of a national park as I have read. He wrote that "a national park should serve men as a reminder of what he almost completely destroyed in many cases and prevent him from doing it again." I am sure the hon. member would admit that this young man has put the case as well as or better than either he or I could put it.
Therefore I am happy to endorse the idea behind this motion and hope that some day soon it will become an item of national policy and will meet the approval of the provincial governments that we set up a permanent secretariat in charge of our park-lands. This is my hope, because what we do today, sir, will influence the welfare and happiness of countless generations of our fellow citizens, of children such as those whose handiwork I have brought to the attention of this honourable house this afternoon.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak briefly in support of the motion which has been put before us this afternoon by the hon. member for Brandon-Souris (Mr. Dinsdale) in respect to the need for an enlarged and broader program of recreational parks which would involve a greater measure of federal and provincial co-operation in this field than perhaps has heretofore prevailed. I thought I might underline the need for federal action as suggested in this resolution by attempting to focus the attention of the house on what I consider to be one of the great, untapped recreational reservoirs of our country. This area I would describe, roughly, as being the western coast of Vancouver island. Most of this area lies within the boundaries of my constituency of Comox-Albemi, though some parts to the south lie within Nanaimo and the constituency of Esquimalt-Saanich. In case the house may think I am taking an unduly parochial approach in my remarks, perhaps I should point out that the area embraced by the part of my constituency to which I refer is roughly the size of the whole of Nova Scotia, and I think most of us are aware that within that province the national parks have at least gained a foothold, which is more than one can say with regard to Vancouver island.
The western coast of Vancouver island is a land of mountains and seascapes, of tree-covered hills and long inlets which some people say remind them of the fjords of Norway. Miles of rocky shore line are interspersed with beautiful sand beaches. It is a land where we have hot springs. There is also a great deal of attractive fishing both in salt water and in fresh water lakes. Yet the whole area is virtually untapped and unknown.
I have often remarked that most British Columbians have never seen the ocean even though they live on the shores of salt water in cities such as Vancouver. The area of which I have been speaking is within relatively easy reach of existing transportation facilities but, as I say, few people now take advantage of its great possibilities. This underlines the need for a broader program on the lines suggested in this resolution as well as illustrating the fact that we in Canada are indeed well endowed with opportunities for increasing the scope of the programs we have undertaken so far for the provision of increased outdoor recreation facilities.
I might point out that this; land is one of considerable historic interest. As far as knowledge of the white man is concerned, it may not be as ancient as the coast of New-

foundland, but its history goes back some distance into the past. It was on this coast that the first landfall was made in what is now Canada from the Pacific ocean when Captain James Cook landed at Friendly cove on Nootka island, one of the smaller islands adjacent to Vancouver island, in 1778. He opened up the era when the white men were venturing on to the shores of what we now know as our country of Canada. Shortly after this, the first economic venture of the white man took place with the development of the sea otter trade between the western shore and China. So vigorously was this "trade" pursued that the sea otter is now practically extinct.
I would point out that on Vancouver island we do have a large park, Strathcona provincial park. This park is referred to less frequently than is Garibaldi park, the other large provincial park in British Columbia. Nevertheless, I think it would be fair to say that the tourist potential of Strathcona is in many ways at least equal to that of Garibaldi. It is a matter of considerable regret to me that the present provincial administration in British Columbia has shown so little disposition, until now at any rate, to co-operate in giving facilities for federal park developments in the coastal regions of British Columbia. I believe that if some of these projects were undertaken as part of a national program developments would take place at a pace in keeping with the need for recreation which is developing in Canada.
